title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (4 of 7)
hook: Patanjali sorts every thought you'll ever have into five kinds, and one of them is sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.3 and 1.4: when the turnings still, the seer rests in itself; otherwise it looks like its thoughts. A crystal next to a red flower. Your line: now. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

Try to count your thoughts from this morning. You can't, of course. Hundreds, maybe thousands: the coffee, the weather, a face from high school, an argument you haven't had yet. It feels like chaos. Patanjali looked at that same chaos about two thousand years ago and did something very calm. He sorted it. Every turning of the mind, he says, fits into one of five kinds. Five drawers for everything you'll ever think. And the surprising part: one of the drawers is labeled sleep.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF THOUGHTS.` → `FIVE DRAWERS.` → `ONE IS LABELED SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Thread five says the turnings are five, and some bring pain and some don't. Then thread six lists them. First, right knowing: seeing what's actually there, reasoning well from it, or trusting a reliable witness. Second, error: knowing something that isn't so. The classic example is one you know from Advaita: the rope in the dusk that you take for a snake. Third, a slippery one: imagination, or knowledge from words alone. Patanjali means ideas that have no real object behind them. The commentators' example is the horn of a hare. You understand the phrase. There's no such thing. Fourth, sleep. That's the surprise. Deep sleep, Patanjali says, is still a turning of the mind, one that rests on absence, on nothing. The proof, the commentators say, is that you wake up and remember: I slept well. Something was there to know it. And fifth, memory: holding on to what you've already experienced. Now here's why the list matters. Once you can name a turning, it has less grip. It's not the truth arriving. It's a memory. It's an imagined scene. It's the rope again. And notice thread five: some turnings bring pain and some don't. Patanjali isn't asking you to hate your thoughts. Right knowing is a turning too, and a helpful one. The work of yoga is to know which drawer you're in, and in the end, to let all five go quiet.
screen: `PRAMĀṆA-VIPARYAYA-VIKALPA-NIDRĀ-SMṚTAYAḤ.` · `RIGHT KNOWING, ERROR, IMAGINATION.` · `SLEEP, AND MEMORY.` · `NAME THE TURNING; IT LOSES ITS GRIP.` · then, large: `FIVE DRAWERS FOR EVERY THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the mind do what it does. When a thought comes, give it a drawer, softly. Memory. Imagination. Knowing. Error, maybe. If you drift toward drowsiness, you can even say: sleep. You don't need to be right about the drawer. The labeling is the practice. Label, and let it go, and wait for the next one. Every so often, notice the quiet between labels. If you pray, you can rest in that quiet. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and threads five to eleven: the five turnings. Right knowing, error, imagination, sleep and memory.
Your line: now. Today, when a worry shows up, ask which drawer it belongs in. Knowing? Or imagination? Then come back to now. Day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras often learn the five vrittis as a list and use them in meditation, noting which kind of thought is arising rather than following it.

fork.setup: you're worrying about a conversation that hasn't happened yet. which of Patanjali's drawers is it in?
options: imagination: ideas with nothing real behind them yet.
fork.reveal: a scene that hasn't happened is vikalpa, imagination. naming the drawer loosens its grip.

original.note: Sanskrit: a turning or movement of the mind. Yoga Sutra 1.6 names five: pramana, viparyaya, vikalpa, nidra, smriti.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means stopping all thoughts at once.
what it means: first you learn to name them: right knowing, error, imagination, sleep, memory.
what a scholar hears: vikalpa, knowledge from words alone; the commentators' example is shasha-vishana, the horn of a hare, a phrase you understand that names nothing.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.5–1.11 (the five turnings, painful and not painful)
Vyasa's commentary on 1.9–1.10 (the horn of a hare; 'I slept well')

notes: Pramana in 1.7: perception, inference and testimony (pratyaksha, anumana, agama); rendered 'seeing, reasoning, trusting a reliable witness'. Confirm.
The horn of a hare (shasha-vishana) as the example of vikalpa and the waking memory 'I slept well' as proof that sleep is a vritti are standard in the commentaries; confirm the attribution to Vyasa.
Viparyaya's example in the commentaries varies (mother-of-pearl as silver, the double moon); the rope and snake is used here because Advaita days used it. Confirm.
